# You're Probably Overpaying to Run Your Marketing — By More Than 70%
URL: https://factor42media.com/blog/youre-probably-overpaying-to-run-your-marketing
Topic: Choosing a partner

Most small business owners don't set out to overspend on marketing. It happens one decision at a time. You hire an agency because you don't have time to run ads yourself. Or you bring someone in-house and buy them a stack of software. Or you cobble together a handful of vendors — one for search, one for social, one for email — and hope they add up to something.

Then you look at what you're spending to get it all done, and the number is bigger than the results seem to justify.

Here's the uncomfortable truth: for a lot of small and mid-sized businesses, the cost of managing the marketing has quietly grown larger than the marketing itself. And when you add it up across all three of the usual paths — a full-service agency, an in-house hire, or a pile of separate vendors — the waste is often more than 70% of what you're paying.

Let's walk through where that number actually comes from, because it's not a slogan. It's arithmetic.


## Path 1: The full-service agency

Agencies are good at what they do. They're also expensive, and the expense is often hidden inside a percentage most owners never stop to question.

Most agencies charge a management fee — a cut they take for running your campaigns — and for full-service and media-company arrangements that fee commonly runs 30% or more of your ad budget. Some structures push higher still. On top of that, many agencies work on retainers that start around $3,500 a month and climb from there, whether or not your campaigns had a big month.

Do the math on a modest budget. If you're putting $3,000 a month into ads and paying a 30% management fee, that's $900 a month — $10,800 a year — going to management, not to reaching customers. Bundle in a retainer minimum and the overhead climbs past what you're actually spending to be seen.

The work might be excellent. But you're paying a premium built for enterprise clients, on a budget that isn't enterprise.


## Path 2: The in-house hire

The instinct here is understandable: if marketing is important, own it. Hire someone. Keep it under your roof.

The problem is what "someone" actually costs once you add it all up. A single qualified marketing employee doesn't come alone — they come with a salary, benefits, payroll taxes, and then the tools. And the tools are their own iceberg: the average organization now runs on the order of 75 different marketing tools, and most businesses use only about a third of what they're paying for. By the time you've staffed even a minimal in-house marketing function and licensed the software to support it, the fully-loaded cost can run into the hundreds of thousands of dollars a year — one widely cited estimate puts a minimum viable in-house department near $587,000 annually.

For a small business, that's not a marketing budget. That's a mortgage on one function.


## Path 3: The pile of vendors

This is the most common path, and the most deceptive, because no single bill looks alarming.

One company runs your paid search. Another handles social. A third does email. Maybe a freelancer touches your SEO. Each one charges its own fee, logs into its own platform, and sends its own report. You end up with seven logins, six dashboards, and no single person who can tell you whether it's all working together — because it isn't. Research shows 82% of small businesses run their marketing through a collection of disconnected tools that don't talk to each other.

Every handoff between vendors is a place your budget leaks. Every duplicated fee is money spent twice. And every hour you spend stitching their reports together is an hour you're not running your business. The fragmentation itself is the cost — one study found businesses waste roughly a quarter of their marketing budget on channels and tools that aren't pulling their weight.


## Where the 70% comes from

Now put the three paths side by side and ask a simpler question: what does it actually cost to get your marketing run — well — across every channel you care about?

Against a full in-house build, consolidating that work with a single partner eliminates the salary, the benefits, and most of the redundant software — the bulk of a six-figure annual cost.

Against a full-service agency, you strip out the enterprise-grade retainer and cut the management fee itself roughly in half.

Against a pile of separate vendors, you delete the duplicated fees and the wasted hours, and you stop paying multiple companies to each do one slice of the job.

Add those savings up against the real, all-in cost of the path you're on today, and for most small businesses the total comes out more than 70% lower — without cutting a single channel. You still get search, social, programmatic, email, streaming TV, and the rest. You just stop paying three different ways to run them.

That's the whole idea behind consolidated media buying: one place to run all of it, one fee instead of many, and a management cost that's a fraction of what an agency charges.


## The catch (because you should always ask)

A number like "over 70%" deserves a straight answer about where it applies. It's measured against the total cost of the alternatives — the retainer plus fees of an agency, the salary plus tools of an in-house hire, the stacked invoices of multiple vendors. If you compared only management fee to management fee, the savings are closer to half. The 70%+ shows up when you count everything you're really paying to keep your marketing running — which is the number that actually comes out of your account each month.

That's the honest version. And for most small businesses, the honest version is still a very big number.


## What to do with this

You don't have to take anyone's word for it — including ours. Spend an afternoon adding up what you're truly paying to run your marketing right now: every retainer, every fee, every software subscription, every vendor invoice, and an honest estimate of the hours it eats. Most owners are surprised by the total.

Then compare it to what it would cost to run the same channels from one place, with one team, at one fee.

At Factor42 Media, that's exactly what we do — we run your entire digital marketing operation across every channel your business needs, consolidated into a single place, for a fraction of what agencies charge and a small slice of what in-house costs. Fewer logins. One report. One point of contact who actually knows your whole campaign.

If you've ever suspected you're overpaying to get your marketing run, you're probably right. Let's find out by how much.

Factor42 Media helps small and mid-sized businesses run every digital marketing channel — search, social, programmatic, email, streaming TV, DOOH, and more — from one consolidated place, at a management cost far below the traditional agency model. Get in touch for a free look at what you're spending now versus what you could be.

# Q4 Ad Ops Without the Burnout: Covering the Holiday Surge
URL: https://factor42media.com/blog/q4-ad-operations-surge
Topic: Seasonal & timing

Every agency knows the shape of the fourth quarter. Budgets that sat quiet all year get released in October. Retail clients want holiday campaigns live before Black Friday. New clients sign because they finally have money to spend. And all of it lands on the same ad ops team that was already at capacity in September.

The agencies that get through Q4 without missed launches or exhausted staff don't work harder in November. They plan Q4 ad operations coverage before the surge starts. Here is why Q4 breaks ad ops teams, which tasks spike first, and how to set up surge coverage while there is still time.


## Why does Q4 overload agency ad operations?

Q4 overloads agency ad operations because volume, urgency and complexity all rise at the same time, while your team size stays the same. More campaigns launch, they launch on tighter deadlines, and each one has more moving parts.

Volume rises because many clients hold budget until the end of the year and then spend it quickly. Urgency rises because holiday campaigns tie to fixed dates. A Black Friday campaign that launches on Monday is not late, it is wasted.

Complexity rises because Q4 campaigns rarely run on one channel. A typical holiday push might combine paid search, shopping, paid social, display and video, each with its own creative versions, flight dates and promo codes. Every extra version is another chance for a trafficking mistake.

Meanwhile, your team is the same size it was in July, and some of them want to take time off at Thanksgiving. The gap between work and capacity shows up as late nights, rushed QA and errors that clients notice.


## Which tasks spike first?

Trafficking and creative QA spike first, followed by pacing and then reporting. Knowing the order lets you add help where the pressure actually lands. The typical sequence:

- Trafficking spikes in October as holiday campaigns get built and loaded ahead of their flight dates.
- Creative QA spikes alongside it, because holiday campaigns carry more versions, sizes and promo-specific creative.
- Pacing pressure peaks in November, when large budgets run over short flights and small delivery problems become expensive quickly.
- Optimization requests climb through the peak weeks as clients watch results daily and ask for changes.
- Reporting and reconciliation pile up in December and January, when every campaign needs a wrap report and every invoice needs to match delivery.
- The mistake most agencies make is planning for the reporting crunch they remember from last January, when the real bottleneck was trafficking in October.


## How do you plan Q4 ad operations coverage?

Plan Q4 ad operations coverage by forecasting your Q4 volume, deciding which work can move to a partner, and setting the handoff up before the first surge campaign arrives. Each step is simple, but they have to happen in order and early.

Start with a forecast. Count the campaigns you launched last Q4 and the ones already confirmed this year. Add the clients who usually decide late. That number, compared with what your team handled in a normal month, tells you roughly how much extra capacity you need.

Next, decide what can move. The best candidates are tasks that are repeatable and well defined: trafficking, creative QA, pacing checks and wrap reports. Strategy, client communication and creative direction should stay with your team.

Then set up the handoff. A partner needs your brief format, access to the platforms and accounts you use, your QA standards and your reporting templates. Doing this in early October means the partner is ready when the volume arrives. Doing it in mid-November means onboarding during the busiest weeks of the year.

Finally, run a test. Send one or two real campaigns through the partner before the peak, so both sides find the gaps while the stakes are low.


## What should a surge partner handle?

A surge partner provides ad ops overflow support: it should handle the operational work that scales with campaign count, so your team's time scales with client count instead. That usually means:

- Trafficking campaigns across the ad servers, DSPs and social platforms you use.
- Creative QA, checking specs, versions and tracking before anything goes live.
- Daily pacing checks and alerts on under- or over-delivery.
- Routine optimization within limits you set.
- Billing reconciliation and end-of-campaign wrap reports in your brand.

Speed and coverage matter most in Q4. Ask a potential partner for their average trafficking turnaround and their delivery rate, not their best case. For reference, Factor42 averages a 12-minute trafficking turnaround from a complete brief, holds a 98.6% campaign delivery rate, and its automated pacing alerts and reconciliation cut manual ad ops overhead by 70%.

Platform coverage matters too. Holiday campaigns often add channels a client doesn't use the rest of the year, such as streaming TV or digital out-of-home, which a partner running white-label programmatic, CTV and DOOH can take on as well. A partner already working across 12+ DSPs, social platforms and ad servers can take those on without a learning curve. If the pressure lasts beyond Q4, outsourced ad operations can cover it year-round; our guide on when to outsource ad operations covers the signs. If the overflow is mostly paid search and paid social, white-label PPC is the narrower fix.


## What does a good handoff look like?

A good handoff is one where your team sends a complete brief once and gets back a live, checked campaign without chasing anyone. It depends on a few habits that are worth setting up now:

- One brief format for every campaign, with flight dates, budgets, targeting, creative and tracking in one place.
- A clear deadline for complete briefs, so missing creative or tracking is caught early.
- Access to the accounts and platforms you own, so the partner works inside your setup.
- An agreed QA checklist that matches your own standards.
- A single channel for questions and status, so nothing gets lost in email threads.
- Reporting in your format and under your brand, ready to send to clients.

The white-label rule applies throughout. Your clients should see your agency and nobody else. The partner works with your team, not with your clients, and every report carries your name.


## How do you know the plan is working?

You know the plan is working when the busiest weeks feel routine: campaigns launch on their dates, QA problems are caught before launch, and your account managers spend their time with clients instead of in ad platforms. Watch a few signals through November:

- Launch dates hit: holiday campaigns go live on the planned day, not the day after.
- Errors caught early: creative or tracking problems are flagged in QA, not reported by clients.
- Pacing stays on track: big budgets spend evenly across short flights instead of rushing at the end.
- Questions get answered fast: your team can tell a client where a campaign stands without waiting on anyone.
- Nobody is working every weekend: overtime is the clearest sign your coverage plan is short.

If one of these slips early in the season, adjust then. Moving another task to the partner in the first week of November is far easier than recovering a missed Black Friday launch.


## The time to plan is now

The agencies that come out of Q4 with happy clients and a rested team are the ones that treat surge coverage as a September or October decision, not a November emergency. If you are reading this before the peak, there is still time to forecast, hand off and test.

If you want help covering this year's surge, book a free consultation. We will look at your Q4 volume and show you how the handoff would work with your team.

# Back-to-School Marketing That Captures the Seasonal Surge
URL: https://factor42media.com/blog/back-to-school-marketing
Topic: Seasonal & timing

The back-to-school season is one of the biggest buying periods of the year — a surge of spending as families prepare for a new school year, and often a broader seasonal reset as summer ends and routines return. Even businesses that don't sell school supplies can benefit, because the season shifts consumer behavior across the board. Capturing the back-to-school surge takes preparation and the right approach. Here's how to make the most of it.


## Why back-to-school is bigger than school supplies

It's easy to assume back-to-school marketing is only for businesses selling notebooks and backpacks. It isn't. The season triggers a broad wave of buying and behavioral change that touches many kinds of businesses.

Families are in a spending and preparing mode. Routines are resetting as summer ends. People are re-engaging after the looser summer months, getting organized, and making decisions they'd put off. This broader shift means all sorts of businesses — not just those obviously tied to school — can find opportunity in the season, if they connect their offering to the back-to-school moment and the mindset around it. The surge is real and wide; the question is whether your business shows up to catch it.


## Preparing for the surge

Like other major seasonal moments, back-to-school rewards preparation. The surge arrives on a predictable schedule, competition intensifies as everyone targets the same families and the same moment, and businesses that plan ahead capture the season while latecomers scramble. Getting ready before the season arrives — with the right offers, messages, and presence in place — lets you meet the surge at its peak rather than chasing it.

Preparation also lets you think through the season's timing. Back-to-school isn't a single day but a stretch — early preparers, the main rush, and last-minute shoppers — and reaching each at the right time captures more of the total surge. A prepared, well-timed approach outperforms a last-minute one every time.


## What captures the back-to-school surge

Making the most of the season means:

Connecting your offering to the moment. Whether you sell directly school-related items or something families need as they reset for the year, tie your message to the back-to-school mindset so it resonates with what customers are thinking about.

Preparing and timing your push. Have your campaign ready before the surge, and time it to capture the season's waves — early, peak, and late shoppers.

Coordinating a strong effort. Rally your channels together around your back-to-school push so it hits with real force rather than scattered activity.

Reaching families where they are. Meet your customers across the channels and moments where they're making back-to-school decisions.

Done well, this turns the seasonal surge into a genuine boost for your business, whatever you sell.


## Why coordination captures the surge

Capturing a seasonal surge like back-to-school well means launching a strong, coordinated, well-timed push across every channel — all working together around your back-to-school message and the season's key moments. That coordinated force is what captures a competitive seasonal surge, and it's exactly what running your marketing as one operation makes possible.

When one team runs every channel, your back-to-school campaign can be prepared in advance and executed across all your channels in concert, timed to capture each wave of the season. When your marketing is fragmented across separate vendors, mounting a strong, unified, well-timed seasonal push is difficult — the effort scatters across disconnected schedules right when it needs to converge. A consolidated setup lets you meet the back-to-school surge with coordinated force; a fragmented one leaves a major seasonal opportunity to scattered, uncoordinated efforts. Capturing seasonal surges is one more payoff of running your marketing as a coordinated whole.


## Make the most of the season

The back-to-school surge is a major seasonal opportunity that reaches well beyond school supplies, touching any business that connects to families' spending and the broader end-of-summer reset. Capturing it takes preparation, smart timing, and a coordinated push across your channels — meeting the surge ready rather than scrambling once it's already peaking.

We help you turn seasonal moments into real business, whatever you sell.

The back-to-school surge is coming. Let's have your business ready to capture it.

# Holiday Campaigns That Deliver: Plan Ahead, Sell More
URL: https://factor42media.com/blog/holiday-campaigns-that-deliver
Topic: Seasonal & timing

For many small businesses, the holiday season is the most important stretch of the year — the period when customers are actively spending and a strong showing can make the difference between a good year and a great one. But the holidays are also the most competitive advertising season, the most time-sensitive, and the one most punishing to businesses that wait too long to prepare. Holiday campaigns that deliver are built on one principle above all: plan ahead. Here's how to make your holiday season count.


## Why the holidays reward preparation

The holiday season concentrates an enormous amount of buying into a short, intense window, and everyone knows it — which is exactly why preparation matters so much. Customers are ready to spend, but every business is competing for their attention at once, advertising gets more expensive and crowded, and the whole thing moves fast. In that environment, the businesses that planned their campaigns well in advance capture the season, while those scrambling at the last minute pay more, reach less, and miss the peak.

Preparation pays off in the holidays more than any other time because the stakes are high, the competition is fierce, and the timing is unforgiving. A holiday campaign thrown together late is fighting uphill against businesses that prepared. One planned ahead meets the season ready — with the right offers, the right messages, and the right presence locked in before the rush.


## What planning ahead makes possible

Getting ahead of the holidays lets you do several things that last-minute scrambling can't:

Secure your presence before it gets expensive and crowded. Planning ahead means you're positioned before the competition peaks, rather than fighting for scraps at premium prices.

Craft your offers and messages thoughtfully. Time to prepare means better campaigns — compelling offers and sharp messaging — instead of whatever you can throw together in a panic.

Coordinate a strong, unified push. Preparation lets you rally all your channels around your holiday effort in a coordinated way, hitting with real force at the right moments.

Build through the season. A planned approach can build momentum across the whole holiday period, capturing early shoppers, peak shoppers, and last-minute buyers alike, rather than a single unprepared burst.

The difference between a holiday campaign that delivers and one that disappoints is very often just how far ahead it was planned.


## The timing within the season

Beyond planning ahead overall, holiday campaigns benefit from smart timing within the season. The holidays aren't one moment but a sequence — early shoppers, the peak rush, and last-minute buyers each represent an opportunity, and reaching each at the right time captures more of the season's total spending. A campaign that thinks through this sequence and times its efforts accordingly outperforms one that treats the holidays as a single undifferentiated blob.

This kind of coordinated timing across the season — rallying your channels around the right moments, sequencing your efforts to capture each wave of shoppers — is what turns holiday marketing from a hopeful splash into a deliberate, high-yield campaign.


## Why coordination delivers the holidays

Holiday campaigns that truly deliver are coordinated, well-timed pushes across every channel — your search, social, email, streaming, and the rest all working together around your holiday offers and the season's key moments. That coordination is what gives a holiday campaign its force, and it's exactly what running your marketing as one operation provides.

When one team runs every channel, your holiday campaign can be planned in advance and executed across all your channels in concert, timed to capture each wave of the season, hitting with unified force. When your marketing is scattered across separate vendors, coordinating a strong, well-timed holiday push is enormously difficult — each piece runs on its own schedule, and the campaign fragments right when it most needs to hit together. A consolidated setup lets you meet the holidays with the coordinated force that delivers results; a fragmented one leaves your most important season to scattered, uncoordinated efforts.


## Make this holiday season count

The holidays are too important, too competitive, and too fast to leave to last-minute scrambling. Holiday campaigns that deliver are planned well ahead and executed as coordinated, well-timed pushes across every channel — securing your presence, sharpening your offers, and capturing each wave of the season. Plan ahead, and you sell more.

# Last-Minute Email Campaigns That Actually Drive Sales
URL: https://factor42media.com/blog/last-minute-email-campaigns
Topic: Seasonal & timing

Sometimes you need results fast. A slow week, an unexpected gap, a sudden opportunity, an event coming up sooner than you'd like — and you need to drive some sales quickly. In these moments, email is often your best friend, because it's one of the few marketing channels that can reach people directly and prompt action on short notice. A well-executed last-minute email campaign can genuinely move the needle fast. Here's how to make one work.


## Why email is the go-to for fast results

Email is uniquely suited to driving quick results for one simple reason: it reaches people who already know you, directly, right now. Unlike advertising that has to find and warm up strangers, email lands in front of your existing customers and subscribers — people who've already shown interest in your business and are far more likely to respond quickly.

That warm, direct, immediate connection is why email can drive sales on short notice when other channels can't. You're not starting from scratch; you're prompting people who already have a relationship with you to take action now. For a last-minute push, that head start is everything — it's the difference between hoping to reach the right people in time and reaching them instantly.


## What makes a last-minute email work

A last-minute email campaign that drives sales tends to share a few features:

A clear, compelling reason to act now. Last-minute campaigns work on urgency — a limited-time offer, a deadline, a reason the recipient should respond now rather than later. Give people a genuine reason not to wait.

A single, focused message. With a quick campaign, clarity beats complexity. One clear offer and one clear action, not a cluttered message. Make it obvious what you want people to do.

An easy next step. Remove friction so a motivated recipient can act immediately. The easier you make it, the more of the urgency converts to actual sales.

The right audience. Reaching the segment of your list most likely to respond to this particular offer makes a fast campaign far more effective than blasting everyone.

Done right, these turn a quick email into real, fast results — which is exactly what the moment calls for.


## The catch: you need the asset ready

Here's the honest catch with last-minute email: it only works if you already have the asset in place. To send an effective last-minute campaign, you need an email list — an audience of customers and subscribers built up over time — ready to reach. If you've neglected your list, or don't really have one, the last-minute channel isn't available when you need it.

This is why the businesses that can pull off effective last-minute campaigns are the ones that treated email as a valuable asset all along — building and nurturing their list steadily, so it's there and responsive when a quick push is needed. The last-minute campaign is only possible because of the not-last-minute work of building the asset. Your email list is a resource you invest in during calm times so it's ready in urgent ones.


## Why email works best as part of the whole

Last-minute email campaigns work, but email delivers its full value — including its power for quick pushes — when it's part of a coordinated marketing operation rather than a neglected standalone tool. When email is connected to the rest of your marketing, your list grows continuously as your other channels bring in interested people, it's better segmented and understood, and a last-minute push can be reinforced by your other channels for even more impact.

This is where running your marketing as one operation pays off, even for something as immediate as a last-minute email. A consolidated setup keeps your email list healthy and growing, connected to everything else, and ready to activate quickly when you need results fast. A fragmented setup, where email sits neglected in its own silo, often means the asset isn't there or isn't ready when the moment comes. The ability to pull off an effective last-minute campaign is quietly built on running your marketing as a coordinated whole.


## Ready when you need it

A last-minute email campaign — with a compelling reason to act now, a clear focused message, an easy next step, and the right audience — can drive real sales fast, because email reaches people who already know you, directly and immediately. But it only works if you've built and maintained your email list as the valuable asset it is, so it's ready when you need a quick push.

Factor42 Media helps small and mid-sized businesses build, nurture, and activate their email list as part of a coordinated marketing operation from one consolidated place — so your list is always healthy, growing, and ready to drive results fast when you need them. We keep the asset ready for the moments that call for it.

Need results fast, or want to be ready when you do? Let's make sure your email is a resource you can count on.

# Summer Advertising Secrets to Keep Sales Hot
URL: https://factor42media.com/blog/summer-advertising-secrets
Topic: Seasonal & timing

Summer changes how people behave, and that shift ripples straight through to your marketing. Routines loosen, travel picks up, people spend more time outdoors and on the move, and depending on your business, summer can be your busiest season or your slowest. Either way, the businesses that adjust their advertising to summer's particular rhythms tend to keep sales hotter than those that run the same marketing they always do. Here are the secrets to advertising well in summer.


## Summer is different — and your marketing should be too

The core insight is simple: summer isn't like the rest of the year, so summer marketing shouldn't be either. People's habits, locations, moods, and buying patterns shift with the season, and marketing that ignores those shifts leaves opportunity on the table.

For some businesses, summer is peak season — customers actively seeking what they offer, and the moment to lean in hard. For others, summer is slow — a stretch to fill with creative effort to keep sales moving. And for nearly everyone, summer changes where and how people can be reached, as they spend more time out of their usual routines. Recognizing which of these applies to your business, and adjusting accordingly, is the foundation of good summer marketing.


## Summer advertising secrets

Whatever summer means for your business, a few principles help you make the most of it:

Match your message to the season. Summer puts people in a particular mindset, and marketing that connects to summer's mood, activities, and needs resonates more than generic year-round messaging. Speak to where your customers actually are.

Reach people where summer takes them. As routines change and people spend more time out and about, the channels and moments that reach them shift too. Meeting customers where their summer actually happens — including out in the physical world — captures attention that stay-the-same marketing misses.

Lean in or fill in. If summer is your busy season, lean in hard to capture the demand. If it's slow, use creative, well-targeted marketing to fill the gap and keep sales moving rather than going quiet.

Plan around summer's rhythm. Summer has its own patterns — holidays, travel periods, local events. Timing your marketing around them captures moments your competitors may overlook.

Adjusting to summer this way keeps your sales hot whether the season is naturally busy or slow for you.


## Reaching people on the move

One thing that distinguishes summer is how much more mobile and out-in-the-world people become. This makes reaching them a bit different from other seasons, and it's where thinking across multiple channels pays off. People on the move can be reached through the channels that follow them — on their phones, on screens out in the world, in the moments and places their summer takes them.

A business that can flexibly reach customers across the range of places summer scatters them — rather than relying on a single channel that assumes people are in their usual routines — captures far more of the season's opportunity. This kind of flexible, multi-channel reach is exactly what a coordinated marketing approach provides, and it matters especially in a season when your customers are less predictable in where and how they can be found.


## Why coordination keeps summer sales hot

Making the most of summer — matching your message to the season, reaching people across the changing places they go, leaning in or filling in, and timing around summer's rhythm — requires the flexibility to adjust and coordinate your marketing across channels. That's hard with a fragmented setup where separate vendors each run their own channel with no coordinated ability to shift for the season.

When your marketing is run as one coordinated operation, adapting to summer becomes natural: one team can adjust your message, shift emphasis across channels to reach people where summer takes them, time your efforts around the season's rhythm, and keep everything working together. A consolidated setup gives you the seasonal agility to keep sales hot; a fragmented one leaves you running the same disconnected marketing regardless of the season. Adapting well to summer, like every seasonal shift, is easier when your marketing moves as one.


## Keep your sales hot all summer

Summer changes how customers behave, and the businesses that adjust their advertising to match — connecting to the season's mood, reaching people where summer takes them, leaning in or filling in, and timing around summer's rhythm — keep their sales hot while others run stale, unadjusted marketing. The season is an opportunity for those ready to meet it on its own terms.

We help you keep sales hot all season long.

Summer's a different season. Let's make sure your marketing rises to meet it.

# Take Charge of Your Yearly Marketing Calendar in Five Steps
URL: https://factor42media.com/blog/take-charge-of-your-yearly-calendar
Topic: Seasonal & timing

Most small business marketing happens reactively. Something comes up, you scramble to promote it. A slow month arrives and you panic-post. A holiday sneaks up and you're advertising at the last minute alongside everyone else. It works, sort of, but it's exhausting and it leaves opportunities on the table. The alternative is a yearly marketing calendar — a simple plan that lets you get ahead of the year instead of chasing it. Here's how to build one in five steps.


## Why a calendar changes everything

The value of a marketing calendar isn't complexity — it's foresight. When you map your year in advance, you stop being surprised by predictable events and start preparing for them. You see the busy seasons coming and build toward them. You spot the slow stretches early and plan to fill them. You approach holidays and key dates with a strategy instead of a scramble.

That shift from reactive to proactive is worth a great deal. Planned marketing is calmer, more effective, and less wasteful than last-minute marketing, because you're acting on a strategy rather than an emergency. A calendar is how a small business gets the drop on its own year.


## Step 1: Map your business's natural rhythm

Start by charting how your business actually moves through the year. Every business has a rhythm — busy seasons, slow seasons, and the patterns in between. Mark your high-demand periods, your quiet stretches, and any seasonal swings specific to what you do.

This rhythm is the foundation of your calendar, because your marketing should work with it — building anticipation ahead of busy seasons, driving activity during slow ones. You can't plan the year until you know its shape, so map the shape first.


## Step 2: Mark the key dates and events

Next, add the fixed points — the dates and events that matter to your business and your customers. These include:

- Holidays and seasonal moments relevant to your business, when customers are in a buying mood or looking for what you offer.
- Industry events or local happenings that affect your customers or create opportunities.
- Your own milestones — anniversaries, launches, annual sales, or recurring promotions.

Getting these on the calendar in advance means you can prepare for them properly instead of being caught out. Half of good marketing timing is simply seeing what's coming.


## Step 3: Plan campaigns around the rhythm and dates

With your rhythm and key dates mapped, plan your marketing around them. Decide what you'll promote and when — building campaigns toward busy seasons, filling slow periods with activity, and preparing well ahead for the holidays and events you've marked.

The point is to spread your marketing sensibly across the year and prepare for each push in advance, rather than cramming or scrambling. A calendar lets you see the whole year at once and make deliberate choices about where to focus effort and budget, so nothing important sneaks up on you.


## Step 4: Coordinate across your channels

Here's a step that reactive marketing almost always skips: making sure your channels work together around each campaign. A well-planned promotion isn't just an ad on one channel — it's a coordinated push where your search, social, email, streaming, and the rest reinforce each other around the same message and timing.

Planning this coordination in advance is what turns a calendar from a to-do list into a strategy. When your channels are aligned around each campaign, the whole effort hits harder than scattered, unsynchronized activity. This is far easier when your marketing is run as one coordinated operation — where a calendar can be executed across every channel in concert — than when it's split across separate vendors who each do their own thing on their own timing.


## Step 5: Leave room to adjust

Finally, hold your calendar firmly but not rigidly. A plan is a guide, not a straitjacket. Leave room to respond to what's working, to unexpected opportunities, and to real-time results. The best calendars combine the foresight of planning with the flexibility to adjust as the year unfolds.

Reviewing your calendar periodically — a mid-year checkup, quarterly looks — lets you course-correct while keeping the benefits of having planned ahead. You get the calm of a plan and the responsiveness of staying alert.


## Own your year

A yearly marketing calendar turns marketing from a reactive scramble into a proactive strategy — mapping your rhythm, marking key dates, planning campaigns, coordinating channels, and staying flexible. It's one of the simplest, highest-leverage things a small business can do to make its marketing calmer and more effective.

Factor42 Media helps small and mid-sized businesses plan and execute a coordinated yearly marketing calendar — every channel working together around your rhythm and key dates, all run from one consolidated place. We help you get ahead of your year instead of chasing it.

Stop scrambling and start planning. Let's build your marketing calendar and take charge of the year.

Factor42 Media helps small and mid-sized businesses plan and run coordinated, year-round marketing across every channel from one consolidated place. Get in touch to take charge of your calendar.

# The Mid-Year Marketing Checkup Every Small Business Should Run
URL: https://factor42media.com/blog/the-mid-year-marketing-checkup
Topic: Seasonal & timing

Halfway through the year is the perfect moment to pause and take stock of your marketing. You're far enough in to have real results to look at, but with enough of the year left to act on what you find. Yet most small businesses never do this — they set their marketing in motion in January and let it run on autopilot, never checking whether it's actually working until the year is over and it's too late to change anything. A mid-year checkup fixes that. Here's how to run one.


## Why mid-year is the right time

The mid-year point has a unique advantage: it's the intersection of enough data and enough runway. Early in the year, you don't yet have results worth judging. Late in the year, you have results but no time left to improve on them. The middle gives you both — a real half-year of performance to learn from, and a full half-year ahead to apply the lessons.

Skipping the checkup means either flying blind or discovering problems only when it's too late to fix them. A deliberate mid-year review lets you catch what's not working while you can still turn it around, and double down on what is working while there's still time to benefit. It's the course-correction opportunity the year is quietly offering you.


## What to review

A good mid-year checkup looks honestly at a few key things:

Results against goals. What did you set out to achieve this year, and where do you actually stand? Comparing real performance to your original goals tells you whether you're on track or need to adjust.

What's working and what isn't. Which channels and efforts are driving results, and which are underperforming? This is the heart of the checkup — separating the productive from the wasteful.

Your spending. Where has your budget gone, and is it delivering? The mid-year point is a good time to catch waste and redirect money toward what's performing.

Changed circumstances. Has anything shifted since you planned — in your business, your market, your customers? Your marketing may need to adapt to new realities.

The goal is an honest assessment, not a pat on the back. The value comes from finding the things worth changing.


## The problem: you can't review what you can't see

Here's where many small businesses get stuck when they try to run a checkup: they can't actually see their results clearly. When marketing is scattered across multiple channels and vendors, each reporting separately, assembling a true picture of half-year performance is a painful, incomplete exercise. You end up with fragments — some numbers from here, some from there — that don't add up to a clear answer about what's working overall.

A proper checkup requires seeing your whole marketing together: all channels, measured consistently, in one view, so you can actually judge what's driving results and what isn't. That clarity is hard to get from a fragmented setup and natural from a consolidated one. When one team runs everything and measures it in one place, the mid-year checkup becomes straightforward — the whole picture is right there to review, rather than something you have to painstakingly reconstruct from scattered pieces.


## Turning the checkup into action

A checkup is only useful if it leads to action. Once you've assessed where you stand, use the second half of the year to act on it:

- Cut or fix what's underperforming, rather than letting it quietly waste budget for another six months.
- Double down on what's working, shifting focus and budget toward your strongest performers.
- Adjust for changed circumstances, adapting your plan to any new realities.
- Reset your goals if needed, based on what the first half taught you.

This is where a consolidated setup pays off again: when one team runs everything, acting on the checkup's findings — shifting budget, adjusting channels, changing course — can happen quickly and in a coordinated way across your whole marketing, rather than requiring you to renegotiate with several separate vendors.


## Don't fly blind for a whole year

A mid-year marketing checkup is a simple, high-value habit: pause, honestly assess what's working against your goals, and use the rest of the year to act on what you find. It's the difference between steering your marketing and setting it loose and hoping. Every small business should run one.

Factor42 Media makes the mid-year checkup easy by running your entire marketing operation from one consolidated place — one clear view of all your results to review, and one team ready to act quickly on what you find. We help you see clearly where you stand and adjust course while it still counts.

Halfway through the year is the time to check your marketing's pulse. Let's run your checkup and finish the year strong.

Factor42 Media helps small and mid-sized businesses see and steer their marketing with one clear view across every channel from one consolidated place. Get in touch to run your mid-year checkup.

# Timing Your Digital Ads Around Your Other Marketing
URL: https://factor42media.com/blog/timing-your-digital-ads
Topic: Seasonal & timing

Many businesses run their marketing efforts as if each exists in its own bubble — the digital ads on their schedule, the email on another, any traditional advertising on yet another, none aware of the rest. But marketing efforts that are timed to work together are far more powerful than the same efforts running at random, disconnected times. Coordinating the timing of your marketing is a simple, overlooked way to make everything you do work harder. Here's how to think about it.


## Why timing matters

Timing matters because customers are influenced by the combination and sequence of marketing they encounter, not just individual pieces. When your different marketing efforts hit around the same time, reinforcing each other, they compound. When they're scattered randomly, each works alone and the reinforcing effect is lost.

Think about how much stronger a message becomes when someone encounters it several ways in a short window — they see your ad, then get your email, then notice you again elsewhere, all around the same time. That convergence builds familiarity and prompts action far more effectively than the same touches spread randomly across weeks with no relationship to each other. Coordinated timing turns separate efforts into a reinforcing wave.


## The cost of random timing

Most small businesses don't time their marketing deliberately, and it costs them in ways they don't see. When efforts run on disconnected schedules:

They don't reinforce each other. A customer might get your email one week and see your ad three weeks later, so neither builds on the other. The compounding effect never happens.

Impact gets diluted. Marketing spread thin and random has less concentrated force than the same marketing timed to converge around key moments.

Opportunities are missed. Big moments — a launch, a promotion, a seasonal push — land with far more impact when all your marketing rallies around them together, and far less when your efforts wander in at random times.

Random timing isn't a disaster, but it leaves a lot of potential impact on the table — impact that costs nothing extra to capture, since it's just a matter of coordinating when things happen.


## How to time your marketing well

Coordinating your marketing's timing comes down to a few principles:

Rally efforts around key moments. For important pushes — promotions, launches, seasonal peaks — bring your channels together around the same window so they reinforce each other and hit with concentrated force.

Sequence for the journey. Time your efforts to guide customers along — awareness-building efforts leading into ones that drive action, so the sequence moves people toward a purchase.

Keep a coordinated rhythm. Rather than random bursts, maintain a deliberate rhythm across your channels so your marketing feels consistent and builds over time.

Align digital with everything else. If you do any traditional advertising or offline marketing, time your digital ads to complement it, so the two reinforce rather than ignore each other.

The goal is marketing that moves together with intention, not a collection of efforts wandering on their own schedules.


## Why coordinated timing requires coordinated marketing

Here's the practical reality: timing your marketing to work together is nearly impossible when it's run by separate parties on separate schedules. If different vendors handle different channels with no coordination between them, their timing is inevitably disconnected — each does its own thing when it suits them, and the reinforcing convergence never happens. You can't synchronize what isn't run together.

Coordinated timing requires that your marketing be run as one operation, where the schedule of every channel can be aligned around your key moments and sequenced for the customer journey. This is exactly what a consolidated setup provides and a fragmented one prevents. When one team runs everything, timing becomes a deliberate strategy — channels rallying together, sequenced with intention. When it's scattered, timing is left to chance. Good timing, like so much in marketing, flows from running things as a coordinated whole.


## Time it to win

Coordinating the timing of your marketing — rallying your channels around key moments, sequencing for the customer journey, keeping a deliberate rhythm — is a simple, no-cost way to make everything you do more effective. Marketing that moves together hits harder than the same marketing scattered at random.

Factor42 Media runs every channel of your marketing from one consolidated place, which means your efforts can be timed to work together — coordinated around your key moments, sequenced for impact, all moving with intention rather than at random. We help you capture the extra power that comes from marketing that's timed to reinforce itself.

Your marketing works harder when it moves together. Let's coordinate the timing and make every effort count for more.

Factor42 Media helps small and mid-sized businesses coordinate the timing of every channel from one consolidated place, so their marketing reinforces itself. Get in touch to make your marketing move together.

# What Political Ad Season Means for Your Ad Costs (and How to Plan)
URL: https://factor42media.com/blog/what-political-ad-season-means
Topic: Seasonal & timing

Every election cycle, something happens to digital advertising that catches many small businesses off guard: political campaigns flood the advertising market, and the increased competition drives up costs and crowds the space for everyone else. If you advertise online, political ad season can quietly raise your costs and reduce your reach — unless you see it coming and plan around it. Here's what happens and how to handle it.


## Why political season affects your ad costs

Digital advertising largely works through auctions — advertisers compete for the same ad space and audiences, and prices rise with demand. When political campaigns pour enormous sums into digital advertising during an election cycle, they add a huge new source of demand to those auctions. More competition for the same ad space means higher prices, and potentially less availability, for every other advertiser — including small businesses that have nothing to do with politics.

The effect is that during heavy political advertising periods, your usual advertising can cost more to achieve the same results, and certain audiences or placements can get crowded and expensive. You're not doing anything differently, but the market around you has gotten more competitive and pricier. Businesses that don't anticipate this can see their marketing suddenly underperform or overspend without understanding why.


## The impact isn't uniform

It's worth knowing that political advertising's impact isn't the same everywhere. It tends to concentrate in certain channels, certain geographic areas, and certain times — heaviest where and when campaigns are focusing their efforts. Some of your advertising might be significantly affected while other parts are barely touched.

This unevenness is actually useful, because it means there are ways to plan around the impact — shifting emphasis toward the channels, areas, and timing less affected by the political surge, rather than simply absorbing higher costs across the board. Understanding that the impact is concentrated rather than uniform is the key to planning around it intelligently.


## How to plan around it

Handling political ad season well comes down to anticipation and flexibility:

See it coming. Simply knowing that political seasons drive up costs lets you plan rather than be surprised. Anticipate the crowded, pricier conditions in advance.

Adjust timing where you can. If you have flexibility in when you run certain marketing, planning around the heaviest political periods can help you avoid the worst of the competition and cost.

Shift toward less-affected channels. Since the impact concentrates in certain places, emphasizing channels and approaches less crowded by political advertising can preserve your efficiency.

Stay focused on efficiency. In a pricier environment, making every dollar count matters even more — reaching the right people and cutting waste so higher costs hurt less.

With foresight and flexibility, you can navigate political ad season without simply eating higher costs and reduced reach.


## Why coordinated marketing helps you adapt

Here's the practical reality: adapting to political ad season — shifting timing, emphasizing less-affected channels, staying efficient across your mix — requires the ability to see and adjust your whole marketing nimbly. That's hard to do when your marketing is scattered across separate vendors who each run their own channel on their own terms, with no coordinated ability to shift strategy in response to changing conditions.

When your marketing is run as one coordinated operation, adapting becomes possible: one team can see how the political surge is affecting your costs, shift emphasis across channels, adjust timing, and keep your marketing efficient through the crowded season — all in a coordinated way. A consolidated setup gives you the agility to respond to market conditions like political ad season, where a fragmented one leaves you absorbing the impact with no coordinated way to adjust. The ability to adapt to a shifting advertising market is another quiet advantage of running your marketing as a coordinated whole.


## Plan ahead, spend smart

Political ad season predictably raises advertising costs and crowds the market, and it can quietly hurt small businesses that don't see it coming. But with foresight and flexibility — anticipating the crowded conditions, adjusting timing, shifting toward less-affected channels, and staying efficient — you can navigate it without simply overpaying. The key is planning ahead rather than being caught off guard.
